messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Nadia was seventy-seven years old, a tutor who had spent decades helping students grasp algebra and grammar in the quiet rooms of a community center. Before the war came to her neighborhood, before the night the building two streets over collapsed in a cloud of dust and screams, she had been a woman who moved through the world without thinking about exits. She had cooked, she had walked to the market, she had laughed with her sister on the phone. That woman, she often thought now, had been someone else entirely — and she had also come to believe that the woman who survived was weak. A stronger person, she was certain, would have shaken off the terror by now, would not still be flinching at sudden noises, would not need to check the locks three times before bed. The fact that she could not let go of the fear felt like proof of a fundamental flaw in her character.

The event itself was not a single explosion but a cascade of them over three days, each one closer than the last. On the second night, the power grid failed and the air-raid sirens stayed silent. She crouched in the hallway of her apartment, pressed against the wall, and heard the whistle of a shell that landed two hundred yards away. The shockwave threw her sideways, glass from the kitchen window sliced her arm, and for several minutes she believed she was dead. When the dust settled and she saw her own blood on the tiles, she could not stop shaking. That feeling — the certainty that death had already touched her — did not leave when the bombing stopped. It stayed, and it became the voice that whispered, *You are too weak to handle this. Other people survive wars and rebuild. You just fall apart.*

Now, years later and safe in a different city, Nadia could not watch a single news report about conflict anywhere in the world. The moment an anchor mentioned a war, her chest tightened and her hands grew cold. She had stopped turning on the television at all. If a student left a newspaper on the table, she turned it face down. She knew, with a conviction she could not explain, that even a glimpse of a destroyed building would send her straight back into that hallway, heart pounding, certain she was about to die again. The memory did not feel like a memory. It felt like the shell was still falling, like the dust was still in her throat. Sometimes she would be washing dishes and a delivery truck backfired outside, and suddenly she was on the floor, gasping, the terror as raw as it had been that night. And afterward, she would lie there thinking, *A strong person wouldn't be on the floor. A strong person would get up and keep washing the dishes.*

She had learned to manage, she told herself. At the community center where she still tutored twice a week, she always chose the table closest to the door. She never sat with her back to an exit. If a student wanted to use a small windowless room for extra help, she said no — she needed to be able to see the way out. The other tutors thought it was a quirk of age. They did not know that she rehearsed the route from that table to the parking lot every time she arrived, counting the steps, checking that nothing was blocking her path. Nor did they know how much she hated herself for needing to do it. She felt pitiful, a grown woman still afraid of doorways. When a colleague asked why she never took the elevator, she made an excuse about her knees, but the real reason was that being trapped in a metal box with no exit made her chest seize up. She interpreted that fear as more proof of her own weakness: normal people rode elevators without a second thought.

What troubled her most, she told the intake clinician, was the numbness. She could not feel joy anymore. When a student finally understood a difficult concept and smiled, she knew she should feel warmth, but there was only a flat, hollow space inside her. She had come to believe that something essential in her had been killed in the bombing, that she was dead in a way that mattered, and that a truly weak person could never recover that part of herself. The thought of trying to remember the event deliberately terrified her — she was certain that if she let herself think about it, she would shatter, and she already felt too fragile to risk it. And so she did not. She pushed the images away, changed the subject when anyone asked about her past, and spent her evenings alone, dwelling instead on the person she used to be: the Nadia who laughed easily, who walked into a room without scanning for danger, who did not check the locks three times before bed. That Nadia felt like a ghost she could never become again, and she blamed herself for failing to become her.

The consequence of living this way had crept up on her slowly. She had stopped calling her sister, because their conversations sometimes drifted toward memories of the old neighborhood, and she could not risk it. She had lost touch with former students who had been like family. Her income had dropped because she refused to tutor in any home that did not have a clear, unobstructed path to the front door. She was lonely, and she knew it, but the loneliness felt safer than the alternative — and also, she told herself, it was what she deserved. A weak person, she reasoned, did not deserve to be surrounded by people. She had let the fear win, and now she was paying the price.

What finally brought her to the clinic was a panic attack in a grocery store, triggered by the sound of a canned good being dropped on the floor. She had stumbled out, breathless, and realized she could not live this way anymore. She was afraid of the help — afraid that talking would break her, afraid that a real therapist would confirm what she already believed about herself — but she was even more afraid of spending the rest of her years feeling hollow, always watching the exit, never able to go back inside, and always knowing that she had been too weak to find her way out alone.
